questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study at a top-university in a non-native English speaking country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall a good experience but nothing out of the extraordinary.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of information from University of Tokyo. They sent email after email with loads of info. However, this made it a bit difficult to navigate in all the rules as there was almost too much information to read through it all.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I had a long email-correspondance with one of the administratives from the University of Tokyo exchange programme (USTEP). They respond quickly and can provide further info. 
I was in doubt with how many courses to choose, which courses I was eligible for etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Private housing (not dormitories affiliated with UTokyo) is expensive. I applied for one dormitory at UTokyo but did not get it at first place. I considered renting an appartment (quite expensive and lots of fees etc., i.e. difficult for non-Japanese speakers), private dormitory and shared housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Housing really depends on what you want. I chose a private dormitory which gives you more freedom (no curfews etc.), but it is still way more strict than in Denmark (girlfriend/boyfriend not allowed to sleep in your room, visitors only allowed until 10 PM, you can't enter other hallways than your own). However, it was a nice opportunity to meet other (mainly international) students.
I stayed in Hakusan House provided by Uninest. It was very expensive and a tiny room, but the facilities were pretty good and brand new. I suppose you could get more value for money, but you would have to look more into private rental and it might be difficult if you do not speak Japanese.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You sign up for courses in a pre-registration period. The first two weeks you attend all possible courses that you are interested in. At the end of the two weeks you cancel the registration for the courses you don't want and you end up with your desired courses.  

There is a course page for UTokyo courses. However, many of the English courses are not available for USTEP students. Be aware of this and select only available courses for USTEP.
The course page is only updated with full course description and possibly curriculum 1-2 weeks prior to semester start.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The UTokyo USTEP office was quick at replying and answered my questions about signing up for courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the courses I wanted from the course list with available courses. I was a first year graduate student during my exchange, but the system is different in Japan so I was a 4th year undergraduate student at UTokyo. This meant I was not eligible for graduate courses which was a pity. There were a lot of interesting econ graduate courses which I could not sign up for and instead I had to choose among a few graduate econ courses available for undergraduates and courses in other departments. I tried asking if I could sign up for a graduate course with help from USTEP, but I was not allowed even though I had done the pre-requisites. I suppose Japanese rules are a bit strict and bureaucratic so do not expect to be allowed to sign up for courses you are not eligible for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Look up all available courses - there are many. I found econ courses at other departments such as Environmental Economics at Department of Agriculture.
Be aware of the requirements from UTokyo as they are different than the requirements from KU. According to KU, you have to do 7 courses as an undergraduate student and 4 (graduate) courses as a graduate student to bring back 30 ECTS. However, these requirements are different when at UTokyo. Here the only requirement is the amount of hours per week: Undergraduate students have to do 12 hours a week (one course is typically 2 hours). That means you have to do 6 courses per week to fulfil the requirements. Some courses are in the first term, some in the second term and some in both terms. Other courses are intensive courses and last only a weekend or a few days at the end of the semester. The intensive courses do not count towards the 12 hours a week goal but you can still get ECTS-points from KU for these courses. So you need to have 6 classes per week during both terms in order to fulfil the requirements and then you might need more classes to fulfil KUs ECTS-requirements. It is quite tricky, but somewhere in all the info given the rules are stated.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I had expected very high academic level, but I was not very impressed with the level. The courses were more superficial than back home at KU. There was a bit of math but the students were not supposed to know any of it. Some courses had a high level but most of them were very easy and did not require any readings and some of the were like advanced high school subjects. 
I expect some of the graduate courses to be high level like at KU, but it is not the case for all of them.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: My courses were fairly small classes with 20-30 students and one professor. The professor did a presentation and depending on the course and the professor, there could be group discussions or standard lectures as at KU. Some courses also had student presentations, I only had to do a presentation in one course. Most courses had many components leading to the final grade whereas I am used to the final exam counting 100% of the grading. In most courses participation (i.e. attending the class) gave points towards final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I had 7 courses (listed from best to worst): "Seminar in International Politics" (= "Contemporary Chinese Diplomacy"), "Japanese Economy II", "Environmental Economics", "Contemporary Capitalism, Financial Crisis, Poverty and Class Struggle", "Development Economics", "Institutional Analysis of Japanese Economy II" and "Start-up and Venture Capital".

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend "Contemporary Chinese Diplomacy" with professor Akio Takahara and "Japanese Economy II" with professor Takeo Hoshi. These courses were very good, probably also because the professors were very good. I would take any course with these professors.

"Contemporary Chinese Diplomacy" might be one of the most interesting courses I have ever taken even though it has almost nothing to do with economics - it is a public policy course. I thought I knew a fair bit about China and Chinese politics but I learned so much and had very interesting discussions with other students. The professor had immense knowledge about China and their historic political development and strategic politics. Since it was a seminar, we had 45 min. to discuss with other students in every class about some suggested questions or whatever else we wanted to discuss regarding China. It was unique to be able to discuss relations to China with students from China, India, France etc. and the other students were very well informed about China.

"Japanese Economy II" was exactly what was needed as an econ-student in Japan since we were presented with many different topics on the development of the Japanese Economy (labour market, industrial policy, monetary policy etc.). Takeo Hoshi is maybe the leading professor at the econ-programme and had written the book on the syllabus, so he gave good insights to all the possible struggles the Japanese Economy is facing.
 
All other courses had no requirements for reading.

"Environmental Economics" was an interesting topic, but unfortunately it was presented in a quite boring way.

The professor of "Contemporary Capitalism" (Manuel Yang) was the most interesting speaker I have had. He was so good at speaking and telling stories and we watched movies and discussed topics regarding capitalism in very laid-back manner. I learned almost nothing, but it was quite fun.

"Development Economics" had a very interesting syllabus but we did not touch upon any of it nor were given the texts. There were no exercises and no slides provided. It was a cozy setting, but the level was very low and I did not learn what I expected from the course.

"Instutional ..." was a graduate course, but I did not understand the professor's English, so I did not attend any of the lectures. The exam was 100% final grade and the material was the professor's own papers on samurai-economics 400 years ago. I found it very boring and a frustrating course to have chosen.

"Start-up .." consisted of a superficial touch on finance, and then we just made up our own fictive firm and did a pitch (in groups of 10). I learned almost nothing.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I expected Japan to be a bit more expensive, but due to weak Yen the exchange rate was very good. This made everything cheaper than expected. Housing was very expensive, but eating out was quite cheap and convenient. Taking the Shinkansen with visitors (who had JR Pass) was very expensive for me, but it is a great experience nevertheless.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are many clubs and circles at UTokyo in all kinds of hobbies. Clubs are more serious and meet up maybe 5 times a week. Circles are more relaxed and might be easier to join as an exchange student. I wanted to play badminton, since I knew the sport is popular in Japan. I managed to find some circles, but some of them did not allow foreigners. However, I joined a circle called Hikousen. It was very fun and interesting to meet locals and speak with them (even though most did not speak English). They were very friendly and I highly recommend trying to join a circle.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Tokyo has just about anything one could imagine. You could play the sport/hobby you usually practice back home, but you could also try something completely new. There are endless opportunities in caligraphy, table tennis, video games, tea clubs etc. I would recommend trying to join some kind of club/circle/thing you want to practice/do. It is a great way of actually meeting locals in a non-academic environment and a big insight to Japanese culture.
Also, go for walks seeing the neatly done Japanese gardens, go into one of the endless small temple sites in the city, go out of the city and to an onsen bath (or sento).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: You could easily spend 5 months only in Tokyo and not have seen it all. Go out to explore new neighborhoods and try to do some trips outside the city. I recommend at least once going to a more rural place in Japan to experience the tranquility and often more run-down places and stay at a Ryokan or Minshuku. Japan and Tokyo are almost two different and separate countries.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
The Japanese culture is very different, and I feel like there are a lot of unwritten rules. However, since Japanese are typically shy, you will probably not be told if you do anything wrong as a foreigner. But do your best to accommodate yourself in the culture, it is very appreciated when foreigners are polite, know a few words of Japanese, don't talk on the trains, line up like the locals etc. 
I found it quite easy to adjust to the culture since it is like a more extreme version of the Danish culture: People mind their own business even more, are more shy talking to strangers and are even more aware of not being in the way of others.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a club/circle.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Probably all the unwritten rules about ones behaviour. The most challenging might be the rules I did not get to know and thus being unpolite without knowing. Try to do your best and they will appreciate you trying to blend in.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How everyone is so polite and helpful. Very friendly place to be.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Check up on the UTokyo rules beforehand.
2. Try to immerse yourself just a bit in the culture and Japanese rules. I suppose it is very appreciated and shows some respect for their unique culture. After a few months you will notice the tourists in the trains taking up all the space and talking loudly, please do your best not to be like the tourists.
3. Don't be sad if you do not get to do everything you wanted in Japan/Tokyo - there are simply too many things to see/do and you will for sure miss out on something.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Trying to live in Tokyo. It is one of the craziest, largest and most unique cities in its own way.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being away from friends and my girlfriend. No matter how much you are prepared for this, you just can't find equal friends as the ones back home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
